prize_parts.citation: for the proposal and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength allow frequency to be measured at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye, and my reasons are now sharper than in round 1. The subject of the prize is one piece of atomic structure: for suitable transitions in Sr and Yb there is a wavelength at which the dynamic polarizabilities of the two clock levels are equal, so the light that holds the atoms does not shift the line. That removes Doppler and recoil shifts and still leaves thousands of atoms in the measurement, which converts a statistical advantage into an accuracy advantage. It is not contained in the frequency comb, which counts optical cycles, nor in ion trapping, where one ion is the oscillator. The idea was then tested against reality rather than only proposed. Katori's group demonstrated it, Ye's group took systematic uncertainty and stability to about 1e-18 and showed the Fermi-degenerate many-body clock, and several laboratories reproduce the numbers and agree with one another over intercontinental links. Millimetre-scale gravitational redshift has been resolved within a single sample, which is a positive experimental result and not a null limit. The theory that controls blackbody, higher-order lattice and collisional shifts agrees with experiment, so the result is understood and not merely working. The count of supporters is not my argument; the chair is right that seven agreeing files prove nothing about the physics. What persuades me is that the objections raised against B004 have each been tested in this round and the strongest of them is answered by the wording of the citation.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 and 2012 remains the real risk, because a reader who knows only that this is another clock prize will see continuity with the comb and with ion clocks. Only the citation can prevent that, so it must name the lattice and the magic wavelength. The tests of constancy of constants have so far produced limits and no deviation, so I would not justify the prize by a fundamental discovery; I justify it by a new capability that is already giving new results. The second has not been redefined, so part of the payoff is still prospective. It remains true that this rewards an instrument more than a surprise in nature, and a committee that weights surprise above all would prefer a new phase or a new observational window. Finally, the SYRTE Sr lattice clock and its contributors, and Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow and Oates, are outside a two-name credit, and any two-name prize draws a hard line through a real community.

responses.point: Danielsson accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate invention from the comb, wants the citation to name the lattice, and cautions that the constants tests have so far given null results.
responses.response: I accept the caution and I change my wording because of it. In round 1 I leaned on the constancy of constants as a foundational payoff; null limits do not make a discovery, and the redefinition of the second can be reasoned about separately. I now rest the case on capability and on what has actually been measured, namely the 1e-18 comparisons and the redshift across millimetres, and I have put the lattice and the magic wavelength into the citation text, as you and I both want. I would still keep the redshift measurement apart from the null constants tests, since it is an observed effect that nobody could see in a laboratory before.

responses.point: Olsson cannot settle whether Katori's proposal or the first operational clock marks the original contribution, and says that if credit cannot be split between two people, B010 is the better-structured alternative.
responses.response: As an atomic theorist I read the original contribution as the proposal, because the magic-wavelength condition is a statement about the dynamic polarizabilities of the clock states, and it came before and independently of any one clock. Katori also made the first Sr lattice clock, so the two things come together in one person, which is why I wrote the citation as proposal and realisation. I do not think it is a reason to move to B010. Your own condition, that two names cannot represent the record, is not met here: the proposal and first realisation are Katori's, and the sustained accuracy frontier and the many-body clock are Ye's. If anything, the B010 attribution problem with Cao and the earlier moire theorists is the worse of the two.

responses.point: Mehlig finds the atomic-structure framing helpful but asks that the committee check the Katori-and-Ye attribution against the history of the first Sr lattice clock, where Lemonde's group, Takamoto and Katori published close together, and that the choice of two names be recorded explicitly.
responses.response: I agree it should be recorded and I will do so here. My reading is that the Sr lattice clock appeared at several laboratories within a short interval around 2005 to 2006, which is the normal pattern once an idea is clear, and that SYRTE's contribution was an independent, early and careful demonstration. It was not the origin of the magic-wavelength proposal, and it was not the source of the later record accuracies. A two-name prize therefore follows proposal plus realisation (Katori) and sustained frontier performance (Ye), and the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and Hinkley should be named in the committee's background material, not in the prize. I will not claim the line is free of cost, but I do not see a case for a third seat that has been made on specific decisive contributions.

responses.point: Eriksson finds the precision and reproducibility argument persuasive, asks whether the 2005 overlap is resolved, and wants twisted bilayer graphene considered for a following year if B004 is distinct.
responses.response: Speaking for the atomic side, as you asked in your round-1 file, I find it resolved in the following way. The comb provides the ruler and ion trapping provides the single quantum oscillator; neither contains the idea of holding a very large number of neutral atoms in an optical lattice with the light shift cancelled. That is a different physical mechanism and it produced a different step in accuracy, which is why the citation must name it. On your own candidate, I think you have made a serious scientific case, and the prediction followed by confirmation is exactly the structure I value. My hesitation is the open superconductivity question and the omission of Cao, not a doubt about the physics. I would be glad to see B010 take up the discussion again once the pairing mechanism is clearer, and I keep it as my second alternative.

responses.point: Kroll agrees on the physics, stresses that the magic-wavelength condition matters only because lattice-induced, blackbody and density shifts are controlled at 1e-18 in several laboratories, and asks what is precisely new relative to 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I agree with the experimental point and with the challenge. What is precisely new is interrogation of a large ensemble of neutral atoms, trapped and held tightly, without first-order Doppler, recoil or light-shift perturbation of the clock line. For the comb the result is a counting technology; for ion clocks it is one oscillator. I would build the citation on that sentence. I take your point that ion-clock and fountain relatives lie close to this, but their accuracy is not obtained with the same mechanism and the lattice clocks have overtaken them in stability by the use of many atoms.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for single quantum systems; I believe so, but I cannot show it beyond the citation text.

Whether Takamoto, Lemonde or another early contributor should be a third name; I have not seen a specific decisive contribution that would require it, but my knowledge of the 2005-2006 priority history comes from memory and not from the documents.
Whether the SI second will be redefined soon; I regard the merit as independent of it, but a redefinition would strengthen the case.
How the committee values a measurement-capability prize against a discovery of the unexpected; the null constants tests mean the foundational content rests mainly on the redshift measurements.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B004: I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. My close collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group and Keller's group does not touch B004 or the two alternatives B036 and B010. I note that I have said in round 1 that I would flag an attosecond candidate if one were shortlisted, and none is. No member has disclosed a conflict with Katori or Ye and I record no recusal.
